title: What boiling water costs in fuel
summary: How much wood, charcoal, gas, alcohol, kerosene or electricity it takes to boil a litre of water, what a household burns in a day, and how lids, windscreens, pot skirts, flasks and retained-heat boxes cut it. Water held at 60 °C for 30 minutes, or 65 °C for 6 minutes, also kills common gut germs, if you measure it. Charcoal and camp stoves make carbon monoxide: they burn outside.

steps.text: Boil at a full rolling boil for at least 1 minute, or 2 minutes above 2,000 m (Health Canada boil water; HealthLinkBC 49b). Much longer only costs fuel.
Cook with a lid on, out of the wind, starting from the warmest water you have (MSR fuel).
steps.warn: Never put a windscreen, reflector or oversize pot on a canister-top gas stove: the can can overheat and explode. MSR's PocketRocket Deluxe manual bans all three and caps pots at 20.3 cm (8 in); read your own stove's manual (MSR PR Deluxe).

steps.text: On wood fires, burn dry wood and fit a pot skirt with a 6–8 mm gap round the pot (Aprovecho HTE).
Keep boiled water hot in a vacuum flask or an insulated box instead of boiling more later (TC 21-3, GIZ WonderBag).
Short of fuel: heat to the first small bubbles, take it off, lid on, and leave it 30 minutes; or hold 60 °C for 30 minutes with a thermometer in the water (CDC Yellow Book).
Budget your fuel: litres a day times the per-litre figure, doubled for snowmelt, and up to 3–4 times outdoors in cold wind (MSR fuel).
Burn each fuel only where it is safe indoors or out; see [Cooking indoors in a winter outage](#guides/reference_cooking_indoors).
steps.warn: Charcoal stoves can give off high levels of odourless carbon monoxide, with much less irritating smoke to warn you than wood stoves (Jetter 2012). Charcoal, barbecues and camp stoves stay outside.

notes:
## What a litre needs
Water takes about 4.19 kJ per kilogram for each degree (OpenStax). Taking 1 L from 10 °C to the boil puts about 0.38 MJ (0.105 kWh) into the water. Starting from snow at −10 °C, you also warm the snow, then melt it at 334 kJ per kilogram (OpenStax): about 0.77 MJ in all, twice as much. These are our sums from OpenStax's figures. No stove gets all of its fuel's energy into the pot, so the real figures below are larger.

## Fuel per litre boiled
| Fuel and stove | Per litre, from about 10 °C | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| Wood, open fire | about 180–200 g | three-stone fires delivered 14–15 % of the fuel's energy to the pot (Jetter 2012); fuelwood 13.8 MJ/kg (FAO wood energy) |
| Wood, rocket or other improved stove | about 50–100 g | several improved stoves did at least twice as well as the fire; the best reached 53 % (Jetter 2012) |
| Charcoal, traditional stove | about 55 g | 22 % efficient (LBL Haiti); charcoal 30.8 MJ/kg (FAO wood energy) |
| Charcoal, improved stove | about 33–41 g | 30–37 % efficient (LBL Haiti) |
| Isobutane–propane canister, upright stove | about 14–16 g | MSR's tests: 1.8–2.1 L boiled per 28 g (1 oz) of fuel (MSR fuel) |
| Same gas, heat-exchanger pot (Reactor type) | about 10–12 g | 2.3–2.8 L per 28 g (MSR fuel) |
| White gas (camp fuel), MSR liquid-fuel stoves | about 18–22 g | 1.3–1.6 L per 28 g (MSR fuel) |
| Kerosene, MSR multi-fuel stoves | about 17–18 g | 1.6–1.7 L per 28 g (MSR fuel) |
| Alcohol (methylated spirit, bio-ethanol), Trangia burner | about 40 mL | a litre boils in about 10 minutes, and 100 mL burns about 25 minutes (Trangia); our arithmetic |
| Propane or butane on an open gas burner | about 25–26 g | an assumption, not a measurement: as efficient as a gas cooktop, about 32 % (Energy Star induction); propane 46.3 MJ/kg, butane 45.3 MJ/kg, lower heating values (ORNL heating values) |
| Electricity, resistance hot plate or coil | about 0.13–0.14 kWh | resistance elements 75–80 % efficient (Energy Star induction) |
| Electricity, induction plate | about 0.12 kWh | about 85 % (Energy Star induction); one lab measured 82 % (GIZ WonderBag) |

Only the MSR and Trangia rows rest on the makers' own figures (MSR's are test results); the others are our estimates, worked from efficiency and energy figures, so treat every number as a planning figure, not a promise. The charcoal efficiencies are averages over a boil-then-simmer test (LBL Haiti). The wood rows use FAO's fuelwood figure of 13.8 MJ/kg, while ORNL lists 19.6 MJ/kg for farmed-tree wood on a dry basis, so truly dry wood would need about 30 % less (ORNL heating values). For an electric kettle, plan on the hot-plate number (our assumption). Real use costs more:
- **Cold, wind and snow.** MSR tests at sea level, 21 °C and no wind, and plans on 3–4 times that fuel for low temperatures, wind and melting snow. A breeze of 8 km/h (5 mph) can triple the fuel an open burner uses (MSR fuel).
- **Snow instead of water:** about double, as above.
- **Wet wood.** Wood at 30 % moisture gives nearly 40 % less useful heat than dry wood (Aprovecho HTE). See [Dry firewood without a meter](#guides/skill_firewood).
- **Cold gas cans.** Butane barely works near freezing: see [Use a butane cassette stove](#guides/safety_cassette_stove).

## A household's day
Get Prepared plans on about 4 L of water per person per day for drinking, cooking and sanitation (Get Prepared kits), so a family of four uses about 16 L. Suppose half of it, 8 L, has to be boiled for drinking and cooking:

| Fuel and stove | For 8 L a day | For a week |
|---|---|---|
| Wood, open fire | about 1.5 kg | about 10–11 kg |
| Wood, rocket or improved stove | about 0.4–0.8 kg | about 3–5.5 kg |
| Charcoal, traditional stove | about 0.45 kg | about 3 kg |
| Charcoal, improved stove | about 0.25–0.35 kg | about 2–2.3 kg |
| Canister gas, upright stove | about 110–125 g, half a 227 g (8 oz) can | about 4 cans |
| White gas | about 140–175 g | about 1–1.2 kg |
| Kerosene | about 135–140 g | about 1 kg |
| Alcohol | about 320 mL | about 2.2 L |
| Propane on an open burner | about 200 g | about 1.4 kg; a 20 lb (9 kg) barbecue cylinder would last about 6 weeks at that rate, and the cylinder and its burner stay outside (see Where to burn it) |
| Electricity, hot plate | about 1.0–1.1 kWh | about 7–8 kWh |

Our arithmetic from the table above. Melting snow for it roughly doubles every line; cooking outdoors in cold wind can make it 3–4 times (MSR fuel). On battery power, 1 kWh boils about 7 L before inverter losses: see [What things draw, and how long a battery runs them](#guides/reference_power_draw).

## Spend less
- **Lid on.** Use a lid and don't keep lifting it (MSR fuel). A lid keeps the air over the water humid, which cuts the heat lost to evaporation (Aprovecho HTE).
- **Out of the wind.** MSR advises a windscreen on liquid-fuel stoves and the WindPro, wrapped about 1.3 cm (½ in) from the pot all the way round (MSR fuel). **Never round a canister-top stove:** MSR's PocketRocket Deluxe instructions forbid any windscreen, reflector or diffuser, and pots wider than 20.3 cm (8 in), because the can can overheat and explode (MSR PR Deluxe). Read your own stove's manual for its limits. Cassette stoves have their own rule: nothing over the can bay (see [Use a butane cassette stove](#guides/safety_cassette_stove)).
- **Pot skirt on wood fires.** A metal sleeve round the pot, with a gap of 6–8 mm, makes the hot gas scrape the pot's sides; Aprovecho rates it as raising heat transfer by about a quarter (Aprovecho HTE). See [Rocket stove from steel cans or sheet metal](#guides/build_rocket_stove).
- **Dry fuel.** See above: wet wood wastes nearly 40 % (Aprovecho HTE).
- **Heat you are already making.** A kettle on a wood stove that is heating the house anyway costs little extra fuel: see [Cooking on a wood stove](#guides/skill_cook_on_wood_stove).
- **The warmest water you can get.** Water from a lake hole needs about half the fuel of snowmelt by our sums (about 0.42 MJ a litre from 0 °C to the boil, against 0.77 MJ for snow at −10 °C): see [Getting water through lake and river ice](#guides/skill_water_through_ice) and [Water from snow and ice](#guides/skill_water_from_snow).
- **Boil for the time that counts, not longer:** a rolling boil for at least 1 minute, or 2 minutes above 2,000 m (Health Canada boil water; HealthLinkBC 49b). CDC says 3 minutes above 2,000 m (CDC emergency).
- **Boil once, keep it hot.** Pour boiled water into a vacuum flask for drinks instead of boiling more later. A hot-water bottle needs hot water, not boiling: let it cool first, fill it slowly over a sink and don't overfill it (Product Safety Australia). The army's steel vacuum canteen keeps water from freezing for 6 hours at −40 °C (TC 21-3).

## Retained-heat cooking (haybox)
Bring the pot to the boil, then shut it, lid on, inside an insulated box or bag and let stored heat finish the job. In tests for GIZ, a retained-heat bag cut the energy to cook rice, potatoes, chicken and vegetables by 22–48 %, and 4 L of water taken to 100 °C stayed above 65 °C for about 9 hours in the bag against about 2.5 hours without it (GIZ WonderBag). The cooking tests ran in rooms at about 31–37 °C, so expect a cold kitchen to lose heat faster (our reasoning). For keeping food hot in a cooler, Arctic Zone says to wrap the food in towels (which also protects the cooler from a hot pot), fill the air gaps with towels, cardboard or crumpled newspaper, and put a blanket over the cooler (Arctic Zone). A home-made box can copy that, but the GIZ figures above are for a bag made for the job.

Cooked food left in a box cools through the temperatures where bacteria grow: see [Food safety: temperature rules](#ref/reference_food_safety/temperature_rules) for how long it can sit and when to reheat.

## Hot enough is enough: pasteurising
Germs die faster the hotter the water is. CDC's travel medicine guide says everything in drinking water that causes illness dies within seconds at the boil, that 60 °C (140 °F) also works given a longer contact time of 30 minutes, and that pasteurisation of food runs at 60–70 °C (CDC Yellow Book). A 2025 CDC journal article says pasteurisation studies in foods and drinks, run at 60–85 °C, typically report at least a thousand-fold (99.9 %) cut in most gut germs, in times from 1 second to 30 minutes (CDC EID 2025). Bacterial spores can survive even boiling, but rarely cause disease (CDC EID 2025).

| Method | Do this | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Short of fuel | heat until the first small bubbles rise from the bottom, take it off the heat, lid on, and leave it 30 minutes | CDC Yellow Book |
| Thermometer (CDC's figures) | hold the water at 60 °C for 30 minutes | CDC Yellow Book |
| Thermometer (SSWM's figures) | hold the water at 65 °C for 6 minutes | SSWM solar |
| WAPI (water pasteurisation indicator) | a small polycarbonate tube holding soybean wax that melts at about 69–70 °C (SSWM's glossary gives about 65 °C); once the wax has melted, the water round it has reached pasteurising heat | SSWM solar |

Getting it right:
- **Read the coolest water.** SSWM describes the WAPI in solar pasteurisation, where the water at the bottom of a black jar is often 5–10 °C cooler than the water at the top (SSWM solar). On a stove the bottom is the hottest part, so stir well and put the WAPI or thermometer bulb in the middle of the water, not against the pot. That placement is our reasoning, not from a source.
- **Water, not air.** A cooking thermometer must sit in the water. An infrared thermometer reads only the surface it's pointed at.
- **Clear water first.** Settle or strain cloudy water before heating it.
- **No leftover protection.** Pasteurised or boiled water can pick up germs again once it cools: store it covered, in clean containers (SSWM solar for pasteurised water; CDC Yellow Book for boiled).
- **Heat does nothing for chemicals.** Neither boiling nor pasteurising makes water with fuel or toxic chemicals safe (CDC emergency).

## Where to burn it
This card leaves the indoor rules to the cards that cover them. In short: only a vented wood stove or a working fireplace sends its fumes outside; a gas range burner needs a window open and a CO alarm, and is for cooking only; a butane cassette stove goes indoors only if its label allows it; charcoal, barbecues, and propane, white-gas, kerosene and other camp stoves stay outside. Charcoal is the sneaky one: after lighting, charcoal stoves can give off high levels of odourless CO with much less smoke than wood (Jetter 2012). Read [Cooking indoors in a winter outage](#guides/reference_cooking_indoors), [Fire, heat and carbon monoxide](#guides/reference_fire_heat) and [Run engines, stoves and heaters without CO poisoning](#guides/safety_carbon_monoxide). Trangia's spirit burner takes alcohol fuels only, never petrol or other oil-based ones (Trangia). Trangia says camping stoves are designed for outdoor use, so cook outside first. If you have to use it indoors in an outage, it asks for good air circulation, not a small closed room, a fire-safe surface such as a baking tray, and never leaving it lit; keep the CO alarm working too, as the indoor cooking card says for chafing fuel. Refill only once the flame is completely out and the burner has cooled enough to hold in your hand, and watch for spills (Trangia). Methanol-based fuel gives off toxic fumes (Trangia). For storing fuel, see [Handle and store fuel safely](#guides/safety_fuel_handling).
